What is Yember and how are its applications connected?

Yember is a multi-application ordering and delivery platform backed by Yember Core. The three Expo applications are Customer, Restaurant, and Delivery; a separate React/Vite web application is the administrator console. All clients call the Go/Echo API under `/api/v1`. Core uses PostgreSQL and validates the installed database against its strict schema contract at startup. The customer app discovers restaurants, builds carts, checks out, and tracks orders. Restaurant operators handle onboarding, catalog, availability, orders, and finance. Delivery partners handle onboarding, availability, assignments, location, delivery completion, and earnings. Administrators manage platform records and controlled operational workflows.

Explain the repository and application boundaries.

The project has three repositories: `yember-core` is the Go API, PostgreSQL contract, migrations, operational scripts, and backend docs; `yember-app` is an npm workspace containing `apps/customer`, `apps/restaurant`, `apps/delivery`, and shared `packages/partner`; `yember-web` is the React, TypeScript, Vite administrator console and its Cloudflare Pages proxy. The customer is a separate mobile app. Restaurant and delivery apps share partner transport/session/UI support but retain separate routes, app identities, and EAS configuration. The admin console is not one of the Expo apps.

How do a restaurant owner or rider create an account?

Partner password accounts use `POST /api/v1/auth/partner-signup` with `kind` equal to `restaurant` or `delivery`; this selects RESTAURANT_OWNER or DELIVERY_PARTNER. The app sign-in flows enforce the matching role. The actual business application is a separate step through `POST /onboarding/application`, which creates the restaurant or rider record and assesses its registration fee. Retrying an existing application preserves it. Partners then upload verification documents, submit bank details, and pay the assessed fee. Fee payment does not approve the application; approval and account activation are separate administrator decisions. Restaurant registration is INR 200 and delivery registration is INR 150, both non-refundable.

What happens during OTP authentication?

`POST /auth/send-otp` accepts `phone` (or the compatible `identifier` field), normalizes it, validates 8–15 digits with an optional leading plus, and requires a configured sender. A one-minute per-phone throttle is checked and rechecked under an advisory transaction lock. Existing unconsumed challenges are consumed before a new LOGIN challenge is inserted. The six-digit code is HMAC-hashed (using OTP_HASH_SECRET when present, otherwise JWT_SECRET), expires after ten minutes, and is sent through the configured provider. Verification accepts `code` or `otp`, locks the newest unconsumed unexpired challenge, compares hashes in constant time, and consumes a successful challenge. Five failed attempts exhaust it. Success upserts a CUSTOMER by phone, marks the phone verified, and issues a session. A missing sender returns service unavailable; local test adapters do not imply production SMS delivery.

Describe access and refresh tokens, logout, and session security.

Core issues HS256 access JWTs with a 15-minute lifetime and 30-day opaque refresh tokens. Only a hash of each refresh token is stored. Refresh rotates the token transactionally, revokes the old token, and links it to its replacement; reuse or expiry revokes the user's refresh sessions. `/auth/logout` revokes the presented refresh token, while authenticated `/auth/logout-all` revokes all active refresh tokens for the current user. Authenticated routes re-read the active user from the database and check that the JWT role still matches. The mobile partner client refreshes after a 401 and checks that the session role matches its app. The admin browser uses a Secure (in production), HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to `/api/v1/auth/admin`; its access token remains in memory.

How does restaurant discovery determine which restaurants I can see?

`GET /customer/service-area`, `/customer/restaurants`, and `/customer/restaurants/:id` accept either both latitude and longitude or an owned saved `address_id`; do not send both forms together. Coordinates must be finite and within latitude –90..90 and longitude –180..180. Core finds active stations whose radius covers the point using Haversine distance. If multiple stations overlap, it selects the lowest station ID consistently. Discovery lists only approved, open restaurants and available menu items belonging to that station. No coverage yields a null station and an empty restaurant list; coverage can exist even when no restaurants are open. Browsing coordinates does not save an address, while cart writes and checkout still require an owned saved address.

How are restaurants and menu categories managed?

Restaurants select an active station during application and their coordinates must remain inside that station's coverage. The owner can manage their own profile, open/closed status, menu items, availability, images, and item variants. Menu categories are global, selected from the administrator-maintained category list; restaurant owners do not create global categories. Core checks ownership, item availability, restaurant approval/open state, variant-to-item membership, and current prices. When a menu item or variant already referenced by an order is materially changed, database logic versions the old record and keeps historical order references and labels intact.

Explain cart behavior and how to add a menu item.

Choose one of your saved delivery addresses before adding an item. The item must be available from an approved, open restaurant that serves your address. Your active cart can contain items from one restaurant at a time; clear it before switching restaurants. You can choose an available variant and set a quantity from 1 to 99. Yember checks current prices again at checkout, so cart prices can change before you place the order.

Walk me through checkout and idempotency.

The customer sends an owned saved `address_id`, a stable `idempotency_key` 8–64 characters long, a payment method, and optionally a coupon code to `POST /customer/checkout`. Core locks the user and cart, checks cart expiry, station coverage, restaurant approval/open state, and every selected menu item and variant, then reads authoritative prices. It rejects empty, unavailable, invalid, or excessive totals. It computes delivery charge from `DELIVERY_FEE_PAISE`, applies an eligible coupon, creates an order and immutable order lines, creates a payment intent, records coupon use, and converts the cart in one transaction. An order number is deterministically derived from customer UUID plus idempotency key; a matching prior order/payment intent is returned on retry. Cash/payment-on-delivery starts CONFIRMED; Razorpay starts PENDING_PAYMENT. Core order prices are numeric rupees while payment amounts are integer paise.

What are the restaurant order states and who changes them?

The restaurant owner reads paginated partner orders and can move an order along `CONFIRMED  →  ACCEPTED  →  PREPARING  →  READY_FOR_PICKUP`, or reject it with a reason. Core enforces role and restaurant ownership and records status milestones in `order_status_history`; the history is not directly editable. When an order becomes READY_FOR_PICKUP, Core attempts to assign an eligible rider in the same station. Lack of an available rider does not itself erase the ready state. An administrator can explicitly assign an eligible rider.

How does rider assignment work?

Automatic assignment considers riders in the restaurant's station who are approved, online, active, not deleted, and have a registration fee marked PAID or WAIVED. A rider with an active ASSIGNED, ACCEPTED, or PICKED_UP assignment is excluded, as is an order that already has an active assignment. Core locks the selected rider with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, preventing concurrent orders from claiming the same rider. Administrators may explicitly name a rider through `/admin/manage/orders/:id/assign`, but the rider must still meet eligibility checks and the order must be READY_FOR_PICKUP. Rejected assignments remain in history.

What status transitions can a rider perform?

A rider assignment normally transitions `ASSIGNED  →  ACCEPTED  →  PICKED_UP  →  DELIVERED`. A rider may reject an assignment while it is ASSIGNED; that rejected assignment remains historical evidence. Picking up is allowed after the restaurant has marked the order READY_FOR_PICKUP. Delivery completion is allowed only when the order is PICKED_UP and collection is settled: the rider must record cash collection, or Core must find a CAPTURED online payment. A repeated request that sets the assignment to its current status is treated idempotently. On delivery, Core updates the order and recognizes eligible earnings transactionally.

How does customer order tracking work?

Customers can read only their own order details and tracking. Core returns a recent rider location only for the order's active ACCEPTED or PICKED_UP assignment and only when the location is less than five minutes old. The rider app posts coordinates to `/rider/location`; coordinates are validated. Tracking can legitimately return no location when there is no active assignment or the last update is stale. The app combines order detail with the optional tracking location; the backend does not promise an ETA or fabricate a location.

How do customer online payments happen?

Checkout with RAZORPAY creates a PENDING_PAYMENT order and payment intent. The customer-owned online checkout endpoint starts a scoped Razorpay checkout flow. Core creates a provider order, then verifies the provider signature server-side and fetches authoritative payment state before recording capture. The apps use a short-lived scoped checkout page so the Razorpay server secret is not exposed to clients. Webhooks are signature-checked and provider state is fetched; webhook IDs and body digests make replay safe. An uncertain provider response remains reserved instead of triggering an automatic second charge. Local mocked tests do not establish live gateway behavior.

How does cash on delivery get reconciled?

When a rider marks a cash order delivered, the rider records the actual amount collected in integer paise. Core compares the receipt with the amount due and stores a cash collection. Cash is posted to CASH_IN_TRANSIT, never YEMBER_BANK. A mismatch creates an exception and holds payout review. Delivery completion requires either this cash record or a verified captured online payment. The rider later records the gross cash handover; the restaurant separately acknowledges the exact gross amount. This acknowledgement is separate from allocating restaurant earnings, and any excess is tracked as RESTAURANT_FEE_RECEIVABLE.

When are restaurant and delivery earnings recognized?

Earnings are recognized only after an order is DELIVERED and fully collected. Recognition uses explicit delivery-fee and restaurant-commission configuration; there is no hidden platform-fee column. Menu/order price fields use rupees, but financial events, earnings, and payout transport use integer paise and INR. Financial postings are append-only, and deferred database checks require each financial event to balance.

How do partner bank details and payouts work?

A partner submits bank information through the finance bank workflow. Core encrypts the account number with contextual AES-GCM encryption and a key ring; a new submission requires fresh verification. Administrators can verify bank details. Payout preparation reserves eligible earning IDs against a verified bank account. The application records a bank-confirmed result; it does not initiate a real bank transfer. A different administrator must verify the bank reference and reason before PAID postings. This separation prevents one operator from both preparing and independently confirming the payout.

Explain refunds and their safety rules.

An administrator requests an online refund with an amount in paise, a reason, and a stable idempotency key. The refund must be tied to the original captured online order payment and cannot exceed the remaining refundable amount. Registration fees cannot be refunded. A request alone does not complete a refund: provider confirmation is required, then an administrator reconciles the provider refund reference. Refund-related earning or payout allocations are held for review rather than silently rewriting already settled liabilities.

What is the database schema and how are IDs exposed?

Core uses exactly 38 approved application tables grouped into PostgreSQL schemas: users, stations, restaurants, orders, delivery, payments, registration, earnings, payouts, cash, accounting, activity, and promotions. The 36 core documented tables plus `coupons` and immutable `coupon_usages` make 38. Each entity has an internal numeric identity for joins and a unique public UUID. API callers use UUIDs; financial relationships use numeric foreign keys internally. Core order/menu prices are `numeric(12,2)` rupees; financial records use integer paise. Startup and migration validate exact tables, columns, types, identity keys, and numeric relationships and stop on extra or incompatible schema objects.

How do migrations and startup schema safety work?

Run `go run ./cmd/migrate` as a separate deployment step. The installer can install a fresh empty database or validate an existing installation; it does not reset data or rewrite installed objects. API startup independently validates the schema contract before serving. Extra application tables or incompatible documented columns stop startup/installation. Back up PostgreSQL and the private document upload volume before deployment. Do not use historical numbered migration files as the normal setup path; the current contract installer is authoritative.

How does the admin web app authenticate and access Core?

The admin console is a React 19, TypeScript, Vite app. It logs in through `/auth/admin/login` with the `X-Yember-Admin: 1` header. Core restricts this route to ADMIN users and validates the request origin against allowed origins. The refresh credential is an HttpOnly, Secure-in-production, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to the admin auth path; the web access token stays in memory. A session endpoint rotates the refresh token on restoration. In production Cloudflare Pages serves static assets and a fixed-upstream function proxies `/api/*` to Core, preserving browser Origin, Authorization, and cookies, rejecting cross-site origins, and disabling caching.
